say.text: A cyanotic 4-month-old has echo-confirmed TOF. Before we read anything off the tracing, a quick prediction.
Which ECG pattern fits?

choices.label: Right axis deviation with a right ventricular hypertrophy pattern
Left axis deviation with a left ventricular hypertrophy pattern
Left atrial enlargement with a left ventricular hypertrophy pattern
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which ventricle faces the obstruction in TOF. The tracing reflects the chamber that is working hardest.
Yes. The ECG in TOF shows right axis deviation, prominent R or qR waves in V1 and upright T waves in V1, characteristic of right atrial enlargement and right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH).

choices.label: Show me the reasoning step by step
I have it, go straight to the chest film

say.text: 'Hypertrophy' without a side feels like the left ventricle, the chamber we meet most often. In TOF the tracing is right-sided: right axis deviation, prominent R or qR in V1, upright T in V1 (right atrial enlargement and RVH).

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look. Name the side first, then pick the chamber and axis.

say.text: Left-sided enlargement is tempting because large shunts load the left heart. TOF is different: the ECG is characteristic of right atrial enlargement and right ventricular hypertrophy, with right axis deviation.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look. Name the side first, then pick the chamber and axis.

say.text: Worked example, step 1. The chain starts at the narrowed outflow. The right ventricle pumps against it, and RVH follows, secondary to chronic systemic pressures.
Step 2. A thick right ventricle and an enlarged right atrium put the load on the right side of the tracing.
Step 3. With significant RVOT obstruction, most blood shunts toward the aorta and bypasses the pulmonary bed.
Step 4. So the film can show decreased pulmonary vascular markings (pulmonary oligaemia).

choices.label: Now you try the last step

say.text: Same infant, chest X-ray now. Steps 1 to 3 are done: the RV works against the obstruction, and most blood is shunted toward the aorta, bypassing the lungs.
Step 4 is yours. What do the lung fields look like?

choices.label: Oligaemic, because blood bypasses the pulmonary bed
Plethoric, because the VSD floods the lungs
Normal fields, but with marked cardiomegaly
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Follow the blood. If most of it goes to the aorta, how much is left to reach the lung vessels?
Right. Most blood goes toward the aorta, bypassing the pulmonary bed, so the film can show decreased pulmonary vascular markings.

A VSD sounds like a lung-flooding shunt, so plethora is tempting. Here the RVOT obstruction sends most blood toward the aorta, bypassing the pulmonary bed. The lungs can show decreased markings, not plethora.

The upturned apex of the boot-shaped heart is due to what?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Go back to step 1 of the chain: which chamber is thick in TOF?
Yes. The upturned apex is attributed to RVH, together with a concave pulmonary arterial segment.
The left ventricle is the usual suspect for an enlarged apex. In TOF the apex is lifted by RVH, with a concave pulmonary arterial segment.

say.text: A big pulmonary artery would make a bulge, so it feels plausible. The film shows a concave pulmonary arterial segment, and the apex is upturned because of RVH.

say.text: Fade three: no scaffold. Your colleague says 'no boot-shaped heart on this film, so it cannot be TOF.'
Reading the wording of the source, what is the fair response?

choices.label: Boot shape is something films may classically show, not a guaranteed sign
Correct, the boot-shaped heart is always present in TOF
The film should instead show a plethoric pattern with cardiomegaly
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Look at the verb the source uses: films 'may' show it. Think about what that allows.
Yes. Chest radiographs may classically show a boot-shaped heart. 'May' makes it a classic possibility, not a requirement.
'Classic' tempts us to read 'always'. The wording is that radiographs may classically show a boot-shaped heart, so it is not guaranteed.

say.text: Last film question. A radiologist describes the film.
Which description fits TOF?

choices.label: Normal-sized heart, upturned apex, oligaemic lung fields
Egg-on-a-string heart with a narrow pedicle

say.text: Yes. StatPearls describes a normal-size heart with an upturned apex, and the lungs can show decreased pulmonary vascular markings.
A named film sign feels like a good match from a memorised list. Build the TOF film from physiology instead: a normal-size silhouette, upturned apex from RVH, oligaemic lungs.
Cardiomegaly with plethora is the pattern we expect when lungs are flooded. In TOF the film can show decreased pulmonary vascular markings and a normal-size heart.
The film and ECG fit, but they do not settle it. A cyanotic 2-month-old has a harsh ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border and right axis deviation.

say.text: Ask which test shows the anatomy directly, without a catheter, and is named as the primary diagnostic modality.
Yes. Echocardiography is the gold standard for diagnosis and remains the primary modality, because it allows direct visualisation of the abnormal anatomy.

say.text: Catheterisation feels like the ultimate, most invasive proof. But the gold standard for diagnosis is echocardiography, the primary modality, showing the abnormal anatomy directly.

Complex cardiovascular morphology: contrast-enhanced CT.
Anatomy plus function, with no ionising radiation: MRI.

choices.label: Cardiac catheterisation as the gold standard

say.text: One of the imaging tests is described as useful for complex morphology. Which one uses contrast?
Yes. Contrast-enhanced CT is useful in demonstrating the complex cardiovascular morphology of TOF.
Echo is the primary modality, so 'nothing more' feels natural. But CT is described as useful in demonstrating the complex cardiovascular morphology, which is the extra job here.

choices.label: Echo for diagnosis; MRI for anatomy plus function without radiation
MRI for first-line diagnosis; echo for follow-up only
Catheterisation for diagnosis; echo for screening only

say.text: Yes. Echo is the primary diagnostic modality, and MRI provides anatomical detail and functional information without ionising radiation.

choices.label: Go deeper: what echo can miss

say.text: MRI is detailed and radiation-free, which makes it tempting as first line. But echocardiography is the primary diagnostic modality; MRI adds anatomical and functional information.
Catheterisation feels like the rigorous test. The gold standard for diagnosis is echocardiography, the primary modality.
Echocardiography has limitations in assessing associated extracardiac anomalies such as peripheral pulmonary stenosis and atresia.
Pulmonary artery assessment matters: repairing cardiac defects without addressing pulmonary artery hypoplasia or stenosis has a poor outcome.
The main or right pulmonary artery diameter should be compared with that of the ascending aorta. CT can also evaluate post-surgical changes, such as patency of palliative shunts.
